lessons.intro: You will learn how to group a short list into chunks so it fits your working memory. Grouped units are far easier to hold and recall than single items.

cards.b: Working memory holds only a few separate items at once. Long lists fall apart because each item competes for the same small space.
Split the list into groups of three. Treat each group as one unit, so nine digits become three units you can hold.
Give every chunk a short label or phrase. A label is easier to recall than the raw digits.

fig.title: Chunking a list
fig.note: Three moves turn a long list into a few units.

ex.q: You need to remember nine digits: 4 8 2 6 1 9 3 7 5. Grouped in threes, how many chunks do you hold?
ex.why: Nine digits divided into groups of three gives 9 divided by 3, which is 3 chunks. Three units are far easier to hold than nine separate digits.

lessons.tip: Group in threes, because three is the easiest unit to hold at once.

quiz.q: How many chunks of three are in 12 items?
quiz.why: 12 divided by 3 equals 4 chunks.

quiz.q: What does chunking do?
quiz.why: Chunking reduces the number of units you must hold at once.

lessons.intro: You will learn to rehearse a sequence so its order stays fixed while you work. Rehearsal in the original order is the simplest way to stop a list from slipping.

cards.b: Repeating a sequence refreshes it before it fades. Repetition in the same order is what binds the items together.
Say the sequence aloud, then close your eyes and rebuild it from memory. If you slip, go back to the last item you got right.
Tap or nod on each item as you say it. A steady beat helps you feel where each item sits in the line.

fig.title: Rehearsal loop
fig.note: Repeat the same order on every pass.

ex.q: Remember this sequence: tea, pen, key, map. Which item is third?
ex.why: Count from the start: tea is first, pen second, key third. Keep counting as you rehearse so you always know each position.

lessons.tip: Rehearse the order out loud, because hearing it reinforces where each item sits.

quiz.q: You hear five words in order. What is the best first step to hold them?
quiz.why: Rehearsal in the original order keeps the sequence intact.

quiz.q: Which sequence keeps the same order as x, y, z?
quiz.why: Only x, y, z keeps the original order exactly.

lessons.intro: You will learn to tag each item with its position number and a vivid cue. Tagging lets you answer what is in position four without replaying the whole list.

cards.b: Give every item a position number as you meet it. The number works like a seat in a row, so you know where each item belongs.

cards.h: Pair the number with a cue
cards.b: Link each number to a vivid picture, such as a key hanging on a big number 3. Vivid cues are easier to recall than bare numbers.
Ask yourself what is in position four. Answering from the number, not from the start of the list, shows the order is really stored.

fig.title: Each item has a seat
fig.note: Each item carries its position number.

ex.q: The list is: lamp, shoe, egg, boat, coin. What is in position 4?
ex.why: Count the items: lamp is 1, shoe is 2, egg is 3, boat is 4. Position four is boat.

lessons.tip: Call out a position number to test whether the item really holds its place.

quiz.q: In the list pear, fig, plum, what is in position 2?
quiz.why: Position 2 is the second item, which is fig.

quiz.q: Why does a vivid cue help a position number?
o: It links the number to something memorable
It removes the need for order
quiz.why: A vivid picture gives the number a memorable hook.

lessons.intro: You will learn why backward recall is harder and how to build a reverse route. Knowing the extra step helps you practise it the right way.

cards.b: You learned sequences forwards, so forward recall follows a path you already built. Start at the first item and move one step at a time.
To recall backwards, you must hold the whole list and then flip it. That extra step uses more working memory than forward recall.
Turn each item into a picture and walk through the pictures from the end. Practise with short lists before adding more items.

fig.title: Forward versus backward
fig.note: Backward recall adds a reversing step.

ex.q: You hear: cat, sun, box, leaf. What is the first word spoken in backward recall?
ex.why: Backward recall starts at the last item, which is leaf. Then you move to box, sun and cat.

lessons.tip: Practise backward recall on short lists first, since the reversal is the hard part.

quiz.q: For the list 1, 2, 3, 4, what is the first item in backward recall?
quiz.why: Backward recall starts from the end, so the first item is 4.

quiz.q: Which step does backward recall add?
quiz.why: Backward recall adds a reversal of the stored order.

lessons.intro: You will learn to hold two sequences together by pairing their positions. Pairing keeps two streams of information aligned instead of tangled.

cards.b: When you must keep two lists, store each one as its own set of chunks. Mixing them without structure is where errors begin.
Match item one of list A with item one of list B to make a pair. Recalling pairs keeps both sequences moving together.

cards.h: Keep one list as the anchor
cards.b: Pick one list as the main one and hold the other as a lighter cue. This stops the two lists from swapping places.

fig.title: Two lists in step
fig.note: Pair items by their position in each list.

ex.q: List A: red, blue, gold. List B: 7, 3, 9. What is the second pair?
ex.why: Pair by position: the second item of A is blue, and the second item of B is 3. So the pair is blue and 3.

lessons.tip: Pair items by position, because matching positions keeps two lists aligned.

quiz.q: List A is up, down. List B is 5, 8. What is the first pair?
quiz.why: The first items of each list pair together: up with 5.

quiz.q: What helps stop two lists from swapping?
quiz.why: An anchor list keeps the main order fixed while the other acts as a cue.

lessons.t: Finding the Next Term in a Pattern
lessons.intro: You will learn to find the rule behind a sequence and extend it to the next term. Spotting the rule quickly is a core skill for keeping track of order.

cards.b: Find the difference between neighbouring items to reveal the rule. In 2, 4, 6 each step adds two.
Once you know the step, apply it to the next slot. After 8 comes 8 plus 2, which is 10.
Check your rule across the whole sequence to confirm it fits every step. If it also gave 6 after 4, the rule holds.

fig.title: Find the next term
fig.note: Each step adds two, so the next term is 10.

ex.q: Sequence: 3, 6, 9, ?, 15. What is the missing term?
ex.why: Each step adds 3. After 9 comes 12, and 12 plus 3 is 15, which fits the pattern.

lessons.tip: Check the rule against the end of the sequence before you trust a gap.

quiz.q: What is the missing term in 5, 10, ?, 20?
quiz.why: Each step adds 5, so 10 plus 5 is 15.

quiz.q: In 20, 17, 14, ?, what comes next?
quiz.why: Each step subtracts 3, so 14 minus 3 is 11.

lessons.t: Swapping Two Items in Your Head
lessons.intro: You will learn to change the order of a list by naming each swap and checking the result. Mental reordering is used in many memory and puzzle tasks.

cards.b: Before you change anything, keep the starting order clear in mind. You need a fixed reference to know what a change has done.
Say which two positions trade, such as two and three trade places. Naming the move makes the new order easier to hold.
Read the list out in its new order and compare it with your plan. Catching a wrong move early stops errors from compounding.

fig.title: Mental swap loop
fig.note: Hold, swap, check, then recall the new order.

ex.q: The order is A, B, C, D. Swap positions 2 and 4. What is the new order?
ex.why: Position 2 holds B and position 4 holds D. Swapping them gives A, D, C, B.

lessons.tip: Name each swap aloud, because a named move is far easier to track.

quiz.q: The order is 1, 2, 3. You swap positions 1 and 3. What is the result?
quiz.why: Positions 1 and 3 trade places, so the order becomes 3, 2, 1.

quiz.q: Why hold the original order before swapping?
o: It removes the need to swap
It gives a fixed reference to check against
quiz.why: A reference lets you check whether the change did what you intended.

lessons.intro: You will learn to break a multi-step reorder of five items into single moves. Splitting the work keeps the load within what your memory can hold.

cards.b: Five items with several moves at once is too much to hold as one change. Split the job into single moves and do one at a time.
Lock in the items that stay put, then move the rest around them. Fixed points reduce how many positions you must track.
After the final move, rebuild the full order from memory. A full check catches any move you forgot to apply.

fig.title: Three moves, one check
fig.note: Do one move at a time, then verify.

ex.q: Start: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Move the last item to the front, then swap positions 2 and 3. What is the result?
ex.why: Moving 5 to the front gives 5, 1, 2, 3, 4. Swapping positions two and three then gives 5, 2, 1, 3, 4.

lessons.tip: Break a multi-step reorder into single moves, and check after each one.

quiz.q: Start: A, B, C. Move the last item to the front. What is the result?
quiz.why: Moving C to the front gives C, A, B.

quiz.q: Why anchor fixed items first?
o: They reduce the positions you must track
quiz.why: Fixed items cut down the number of positions still in motion.

lessons.t: Why Old Items Interfere With New
lessons.intro: You will learn why old information interferes with new information stored in the same slot. Recognising this interference helps you avoid wrong answers after an update.

cards.b: When you learn something new in the same slot, the old version often stays active. That old version competes with the update and causes errors.
Interference shows up as a wrong answer that feels familiar. When you catch that feeling, you know the old item is leaking into the new one.
Mark the new value clearly, such as with the word now or latest. A clear label tells memory which version to keep.

fig.title: How an update clashes
fig.note: The old item must be released for the new one to win.

ex.q: Your locker code was 4917. Today it changed to 2054. Which code should you enter?
ex.why: The change replaces the old code, so the current code is 2054. The old 4917 no longer applies.

lessons.tip: Say the new one is out loud when you update, so the old item loses its hold.

quiz.q: A meeting room changed from B4 to C2. Which room do you go to?
quiz.why: The update replaces B4, so C2 is the current room.

quiz.q: What usually causes an old item to interfere?
o: Old and new items sharing one slot
quiz.why: When an old and a new value compete for one slot, the old one can leak through.

lessons.intro: You will learn to replace one value cleanly instead of stacking the new one on the old. Clean replacement stops your memory from carrying two versions at once.

cards.b: Treat an update as a swap, not an extra item. Stacking the new value on the old one doubles the load on your memory.
Say the old value once before you let it go. Naming it lets you drop it on purpose instead of holding both.
After the update, rehearse just the new value a few times. Repetition strengthens the new value while the old trace weakens.

fig.title: Swap, do not stack
fig.note: Replace the value, never keep both.

ex.q: A parking space was changed from 12 to 18. Which space do you drive to?
ex.why: The update replaces 12, so the current space is 18. Holding 12 as well would send you to the wrong place.

lessons.tip: Say the old value once, then let it go, because naming it helps you release it.

quiz.q: Your meeting moved from 3pm to 4pm. What should you hold in mind?
quiz.why: The update replaces 3pm, so only the new 4pm stays active.

quiz.q: Which step makes an update stick best?
quiz.why: Rehearsing the new value strengthens it while the old one fades.

lessons.t: Replacing an Item in a List
lessons.intro: You will learn to find the exact slot of an item and swap in its replacement. Changing only the right position keeps the rest of the list stable.

cards.b: Locate the position of the item you are replacing before you change it. Knowing its place means the new item goes where the old one was.

cards.h: Swap in place, keep the rest
cards.b: Put the new item into that exact position and leave the other items alone. Changing only one slot keeps the rest of the list stable.
Recite the whole list once to check the update. A quick full run confirms the replacement sits correctly among the others.

fig.title: Jam swapped for honey
fig.note: Position two now holds honey, not jam.

ex.q: The list is pen, cup, key, map. Replace key with coin. Which list is right?
ex.why: Key sits in position three, so coin takes that place. The other items stay where they are.

lessons.tip: Find the slot before you swap, because the new item belongs where the old one was.

quiz.q: The list is red, green, blue. Replace green with gold. What is the second item?
quiz.why: Green sat in position two, so gold now takes that place.

quiz.q: Why recite the whole list after a swap?
o: To confirm the replacement sits correctly
quiz.why: A full run shows whether the new item sits correctly among the others.

lessons.intro: You will learn to keep one running total and update it after each change. Holding a single current value is far lighter than tracking every step.

cards.b: When numbers change, hold only the current total rather than every step. One updated number is far lighter than a long chain.

cards.h: Apply each change to the total
cards.b: Take the current total, apply one change, and let the result replace it. Then move to the next change and repeat.
Round the numbers to quick values and see whether your result is close. A rough estimate catches big slips in the running total.

fig.title: Running total
fig.note: Each change replaces the total before the next one.

ex.q: Start at 20. Add 6, then take away 4. What is the total?
ex.why: 20 plus 6 is 26. Then 26 minus 4 is 22, so the running total ends at 22.

lessons.tip: Replace the total after each change, so you never hold two totals at once.

quiz.q: The total is 50. Add 9, then subtract 12. What is the total?
quiz.why: 50 plus 9 is 59, and 59 minus 12 is 47.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of a running total?
o: It needs only the current value
quiz.why: Holding one current value is much lighter than holding the full history.

lessons.intro: You will learn to revise a plan when new facts arrive. Updating your plan early stops you acting on information that is no longer true.

cards.b: When new information comes in, your earlier plan may no longer fit. Accept the update early rather than clinging to the old route.
Name the part of the plan that no longer holds. Marking it as out of date stops it from quietly guiding your next step.
Say the new plan in one sentence before you act. One clear sentence is easier to hold than the whole history of changes.

fig.title: Update the plan early
fig.note: Revise as soon as a fact changes the route.

ex.q: Your plan: meet at 10 at the station. New fact: the station is closed, so meet at the library at 10. Where do you go at 10?
ex.why: The new fact replaces the station with the library. The station plan is now out of date.

lessons.tip: Restate the revised plan in one sentence, because one clear sentence replaces a long history.

quiz.q: Your recipe said bake at 180 degrees, and now says 200. Which temperature do you use?
quiz.why: The update replaces the old 180 with the new 200.

quiz.q: What should you do first when a plan changes?
quiz.why: Marking what is now false stops it from quietly guiding your next step.

lessons.intro: You will learn to relabel items when a rule changes partway through a task. Applying the new rule to everything already done prevents mixed-up answers.

cards.b: A task may change its rule partway through, such as a new colour for the same group. Your job is to replace the old label with the new one for every item.
Go back through the items you already sorted and apply the new label. Leaving some items with the old label causes mixed-up answers.

cards.h: Hold the new rule in one line
cards.b: Keep the rule in one short sentence, such as even is blue now. A short rule is easier to apply than the full history of changes.

fig.title: Recoloured after a rule change
fig.note: Evens are now blue and odds are grey.

ex.q: Old rule: odd numbers are red. New rule: odd numbers are green. What colour is 7 now?
ex.why: The new rule replaces the old one, so odd numbers, including 7, are now green.

lessons.tip: Apply a rule change to everything already sorted, not only to new items.

quiz.q: Old rule: squares score 2. New rule: squares score 5. What is the score for a square now?
quiz.why: The new rule replaces 2 with 5.

quiz.q: After a rule change, what must you update?
quiz.why: Items labelled under the old rule now carry the wrong label.

lessons.intro: You will learn to track several updates to one value in their correct order. Following the order makes sure you use the latest value and not an earlier one.

cards.b: A value may change more than once, such as a price rising and then falling. Each change replaces the last, so only the most recent value counts.
Label the updates first, second and third as they arrive. Ordering them stops an earlier change from overriding a later one.
Before answering, look for the final update and use that value. Going back to an earlier value is a common slip under pressure.

fig.title: Latest value wins
fig.note: Only the most recent update counts as current.

ex.q: A price was 10, then rose to 12, then fell to 9. What is the current price?
ex.why: The latest update is the fall to 9, which replaces the earlier 10 and 12.

lessons.tip: Find the most recent update first, because it overrides all the earlier ones.

quiz.q: A timer was set to 5 minutes, changed to 8, then changed to 6. What is it now?
quiz.why: The last change sets the timer to 6, which replaces the earlier 5 and 8.

quiz.q: Why label updates by order?
o: So the latest one is clear
quiz.why: An ordered label shows which update came last.

lessons.intro: You will learn to track several slots at once and audit them at the end. A simple map of current values keeps many updates under control.

cards.b: With several items changing, keep a simple map of each slot and its current value. A map lets you update one slot without disturbing the others.
For each update, say the slot and the new value before overwriting the old one. Stating it first keeps every change accountable.

cards.h: Audit the board at the end
cards.b: After all updates, read every slot back and compare it with your latest notes. A final audit catches a value that was never refreshed.

fig.title: Board after updates
fig.note: C was 2, then changed to 5. B was 7, then became 3.

ex.q: Slots: A=4, B=7, C=2. Update 1: C becomes 5. Update 2: B becomes 3. What is the value of C?
ex.why: Update 1 replaces C's 2 with 5. Update 2 changes only B, so C stays at 5.

lessons.tip: Read every slot back after the last update, because a missed refresh hides in plain sight.

quiz.q: X=1, Y=6. Update: X becomes 4. What is X now?
quiz.why: The update replaces 1 with 4.

quiz.q: Why audit the board at the end?
quiz.why: A final read-back exposes any value that never got its update.

lessons.intro: You will learn what an interruption does to a list you are holding. Knowing the cost helps you plan for breaks instead of being caught out by them.

cards.b: A sudden question or noise can push held items out of working memory. The items do not vanish at once, but they become harder to reach.
Each switch away from a task takes a moment to re-orient. Short switches add up when you change tasks many times.
Before you respond to an interruption, note exactly where you were. A clear marker lets you resume without starting over.

fig.title: With and without a break
fig.note: Interruptions raise the chance of slips.

ex.q: You are holding red, blue, green when someone asks you a question. What should you do first?
ex.why: Noting your place, such as next is green, lets you resume the list afterwards. Without that marker you may lose the order.

lessons.tip: Mark your place in one word, such as next, so the return is quick.

quiz.q: After an interruption, what helps you resume a list?
o: Knowing the last item you held
quiz.why: The last item you held tells you exactly where the list continues.

quiz.q: What does a task switch cost?
quiz.why: A switch takes a moment to re-orient, though the delay is usually small.

lessons.intro: You will learn to keep your place in a list while you pause. A clear marker lets you resume quickly and accurately.

cards.h: Hold the list and the pause
cards.b: Keep the list in memory when you pause, and note its last item. Holding both the list and its end point makes resuming simple.
Attach a cue such as after green to your position. The cue points you straight back to where you stopped.
Run through the list from its start once you return, then continue from the marker. A brief rehearsal reloads the order before you go on.

fig.title: Pause and resume loop
fig.note: Hold the list, pause, answer, then pick up at the marker.

ex.q: You recite 2, 5, 8, 11, 14. You stop after 8. What number comes next when you resume?
ex.why: The list continues after 8, and 8 plus 3 is 11, so the next number is 11.

lessons.tip: Pick a one-word end cue, because a single word is quick to retrieve after a break.

quiz.q: You stop a list at cup. The list was cap, cup, cat. What comes next?
quiz.why: Cat follows cup in the original order.

quiz.q: Why rehearse the start after an interruption?
o: It reloads the order before continuing
quiz.why: A brief run from the start reloads the order before you carry on.

lessons.intro: You will learn to filter out irrelevant items while you hold the ones that matter. Filtering stops noise from taking a place in your memory.

cards.b: Before the distractions arrive, define which items matter for the task. A clear rule lets you discard the rest without thinking.
When a distracting item appears, label it as noise and let it go. Naming it as noise stops it from taking a place in your list.
Train with lists that mix relevant items and noise, such as digits among symbols. Repetition builds a habit of filtering quickly.

fig.title: Ignore the noise
fig.note: Only digits count. Symbols are noise to discard.

ex.q: Remember only the numbers in: A, 3, #, 8, b, 5. How many numbers must you hold?
ex.why: The numbers are 3, 8 and 5, so there are three. A, #, and b are noise.

lessons.tip: Decide the filter rule before the list starts, so noise never gets a place.

quiz.q: From x, 4, y, 6, which items do you hold for a number-only task?
quiz.why: 4 and 6 are the numbers, while x and y are noise.

quiz.q: What is the best way to handle a distracting item?
o: Label it as noise and let it go
quiz.why: Naming it as noise keeps it from taking a place in the list.

lessons.t: Holding a List While Doing Another Task
lessons.intro: You will learn how a second task competes with a list you are holding. Managing that competition keeps your recall reliable.

cards.b: Doing a second task while holding a list divides your attention. Each part gets less capacity, so errors in the list rise.
Keep the second task simple, such as counting by twos, so it needs little thought. An automatic task leaves more room for the list.
Glance back at the list between steps of the other task. Short checks keep the list fresh without stopping the second task.

fig.title: Illustrative attention load
fig.note: Illustrative units, not measured data.

ex.q: You hold red, blue, green while doing a simple counting task. Which approach keeps the list most secure?
o: Ignore the list until the count ends
Check the list between count steps
ex.why: Short checks between count steps keep the list fresh. Ignoring it until the end risks losing the order.

lessons.tip: Keep the second task simple, because automatic actions need less of your attention.

quiz.q: Why does a second task raise list errors?
o: It adds items to the list
quiz.why: Two tasks share the same limited attention.

quiz.q: Which second task is least demanding?
quiz.why: A single repeated word needs almost no thought, so it leaves room for the list.

lessons.intro: You will learn to resist a habitual answer when the rule has changed. Pausing to name the current rule protects you from automatic errors.

cards.b: Under pressure, the answer you used most often tends to come up first. That pull is strong even when the rule has changed.
Take one beat to ask what the rule is now. The pause gives controlled thinking time to override the habit.
Say the current rule before you respond, such as odd means left. Naming the rule keeps it active over the habit.

fig.title: Automatic versus controlled

pts: Often wrong after a rule change

fig.note: A brief pause lets the current rule win.

ex.q: Rule now: if a number is odd, press left. If even, press right. The number is 9. What do you press?
ex.why: 9 is odd, and the current rule says odd means left. The old habit may say right, so pause to check.

lessons.tip: Say the current rule before you act, because naming it beats the old habit.

quiz.q: Rule now: a tick goes to a number divisible by 5. Which gets a tick: 12, 21, or 15?
quiz.why: Only 15 is divisible by 5 of the three numbers.

quiz.q: What does the pause before answering do?
o: Gives controlled thinking time to check the rule
quiz.why: The pause gives controlled thinking the chance to override the habit.

lessons.intro: You will learn how background noise affects accuracy and how to reduce its effect. Small changes to your surroundings can protect the items you hold.

cards.b: Sounds and visual clutter use up some of the attention you need for holding items. The same list becomes harder to keep exact.
Clear your immediate surroundings and close unneeded tabs before a memory task. Less competition means more of your capacity goes to the list.
In a noisy setting, read back your answer before you commit to it. A quick recheck catches errors that noise caused.

fig.title: Items kept out of 5
fig.note: Illustrative scores, not measured data.

ex.q: You hold 4 numbers in quiet and recall all 4. In noise you recall 3. How many numbers did the noise cost you?
ex.why: Four minus three is one, so the noise cost you one number.

lessons.tip: Clear the clutter before you start, since less competition leaves more room for the list.

quiz.q: A list of 5 is recalled as 4 in noise. How many were lost?
quiz.why: Five minus four is one.

quiz.q: What is a good step before a memory task in a busy room?
quiz.why: Removing nearby distractions frees capacity for the items you hold.

lessons.t: Rebuilding a Lost Item in a List
lessons.intro: You will learn to rebuild a missing item from its neighbours in a list. Rebuilding lets you keep going instead of abandoning the whole sequence.

cards.h: A gap is not the end
cards.b: Losing one item mid-list does not mean losing the whole sequence. The items on either side still anchor where the gap belongs.
Look at the items just before and after the gap and ask what fits between them. Neighbouring items often pin down the missing one.
Put your best reconstruction in place, then recite the list to test it. Checking the full run confirms the rebuilt item fits.

fig.title: Rebuild from neighbours
fig.note: Use the items on either side to find the gap.

ex.q: The list is Ant, Bee, ?, Dog, Elk in alphabetical order. Which word fills the gap?
ex.why: The gap must start with C to sit between Bee and Dog. Cat fits, while Dove, Ape and Eel start with the wrong letters for that place.

lessons.tip: Read the neighbours on both sides before you guess, because they narrow the gap.

quiz.q: The list is Ant, ?, Cat. Which word fills the gap?
quiz.why: Bee starts with B, which sits between A and C.

quiz.q: What do you do after rebuilding a gap?
o: Recite the full list to test it
quiz.why: Reciting the whole list confirms the rebuilt item fits.

lessons.intro: You will learn to resume a task at a clear checkpoint after interruptions. Checkpoints stop you from repeating or skipping steps when you return.

cards.b: Record the last step you finished before any interruption. A checkpoint turns a messy return into a single clear restart point.
The first moment after returning is when slips are most likely. Slow down for the opening items and check each one.
If you wrote the state down, compare your recall with the note before you proceed. The written note catches drift that memory may have introduced.

fig.title: Checkpoint after each step
fig.note: Resume at the highlighted step after a break.

ex.q: Your checkpoint says steps 1 to 3 are done. After an interruption, which step do you resume at?
ex.why: Steps 1 to 3 are complete, so the next unfinished step is step 4.

lessons.tip: Write a one-word checkpoint before each break, so return means picking up at a known point.

quiz.q: Your checkpoint says done through item 6. Where do you resume?
quiz.why: Resume at 7, the item after the last one finished.

quiz.q: Why check notes after a return?
quiz.why: A written note exposes any detail your memory has shifted.

lessons.intro: You will learn to combine chunking, tagging, filtering and checkpoints under sustained distraction. Layered methods keep accuracy high when a single method is not enough.

cards.b: Chunk the items, tag their positions, filter noise and checkpoint breaks. Layering the methods covers the weak point of each one.
Decide in advance what to protect first, such as list order over side details. A ranked list tells you what to drop when load peaks.
After a long distracted task, recheck key items against the original source. Auditing against the source is your last defence against drift.

fig.title: Strategies compared
fig.note: Layering covers the weak point of each method.

ex.q: You chunk 12 digits into groups of three. How many chunks do you hold?
ex.why: 12 divided by 3 is 4, so you hold four chunks, each one easy to tag and checkpoint.

lessons.tip: Layer your methods, since each one covers a weakness the others leave open.

quiz.q: Which pairing best protects accuracy under interruption?
quiz.why: Chunks keep the load small and checkpoints keep your place.

quiz.q: What should you drop first when load peaks?
quiz.why: Ranked priorities tell you which low-value detail to let go.
